paras: The Covington lynching threat against Will Smith took place in Covington, Georgia, on the afternoon of December 23, 1882, when a large crowd met Sheriff Anderson bringing in Smith, who was accused of two shootings, and cried for him to be killed and hanged. The sheriff got Smith to jail through the crowd, and a strong guard was posted. Southern papers headed the story as a lynching threatened or in prospect, while short wires elsewhere reported only the killings.

According to the Atlanta dispatch, Will Smith of Jasper and James Banks of the county met in a Covington barroom about 3 o'clock on Saturday afternoon and quarreled over cards. Smith pressed a scuffle that Banks declined, then shot Banks through the body with a navy six-shooter, and Banks staggered out and died at the next door. Short wires gave Smith's age as 18 and blamed whiskey; none of the papers stated his race.

Smith fled, pursued by "white and colored men," and when Alexander Hendricks, identified as "colored," overtook him with a rock in his hand and ordered him to stop, Smith shot him through the body. The Daily Gazette's version said Hendricks died within a few moments, and another pursuer then fired at Smith and put a ball through his hat. About a mile out of town Smith hid behind a pile of brush, and Sheriff Anderson rode up and demanded his surrender.

When the sheriff arrived in town with his prisoner, "a yell was raised" and the crowd ran toward them shouting "kill him!" and "Let's hang him!" With a large crowd in the streets, Smith was brought to the jail only with difficulty. The dispatch closed that the excitement was still high, a strong guard was on duty, and "the law will be executed."
No report that the crowd took Smith from the jail, and no report of an inquest, indictment or trial, appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News ran the full dispatch on December 25 under the headline "Threatened with Lynching," and the Daily Gazette carried a version dated December 25 as "Two Men Killed and a Lynching in Prospect." The Knoxville Daily Chronicle headed the same text "Cards and Whisky Kill Two Men, and will Hang a Third," anticipating Smith's hanging.

A shorter Atlanta wire, printed by the New York Sun as "A Youth Kills Three Men" and reprinted in Montana, Washington, Nevada and Ohio, said Smith had killed Banks, Hendricks and "a negro who attempted to arrest him," and made no mention of a lynching threat.

The short wire counted three dead while the detailed dispatch named only Banks and Hendricks, and the third man in the wire may be Hendricks counted twice. Dispatches dated December 23 put the shooting on that day, while one dated December 25 called it "yesterday"; the Savannah and Knoxville texts had the sheriff arriving with a posse, while the Gazette said he took Smith alone.
